answers: A brief, planned ceasefire failed to materialize in Gaza today, as death continued to rain down on the strip. Israel had offered to hold its offensive to accommodate a visit from Egyptian Prime Minister Hesham Kandil, provided Hamas held its fire as well. But Hamas said it would keep firing, and one Israeli defense minister complained that 50 rockets had flown in from Gaza during Kandil's visit, CNN reports. A Hamas-run TV station reported that Israel had kept firing as well, but Israel says it took a break for at least two hours. In Palestine the death toll has risen to 21, including 13 civilians, Reuters reports. Among those civilians were seven children and a pregnant teenager. Israel's death toll held steady at 3, despite the hundreds of rockets fired into Israel. But Hamas did up the ante by firing rockets near Tel Aviv for the first time. Air-raid sirens sounded (the last time they did so was during the Gulf War) and civilians ran for cover, though the missiles exploded harmlessly, with one going into the sea. "There will be a price for that escalation," Ehud Barak vowed, according to the New York Times. Israel has now hit 250 Gaza targets, while taking further steps toward a ground invasion, calling up 16,000 reservists, the Wall Street Journal reports. It's also steadily sending troops and armored vehicles to the border, notes CNN—between 1,500 and 2,000 are already there, one official said. Israel claims the attacks have weakened Hamas' military capabilities and caused its attacks to lighten, but Hamas denied that, saying it had hit multiple Israeli targets today. Kandil emerged from his meeting with Hamas expressing solidarity, saying the new Egyptian regime would be more active in helping the Palestinians. "The time has changed," he said. "No longer the Israeli occupation will be able to carry out their attacks against the Palestinians without being held responsible. That time is far bygone." For its part, the Obama administration says it's seeking help from Arab countries in calling on Hamas to relent. "The onus rests squarely on Hamas ... to stop its rocket attacks," says a State Department spokesman. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-Moon is planning diplomatic visits to Jerusalem, Ramallah, and Cairo within days.

The situation in the Israel-Gaza conflict has escalated dramatically, with both sides intensifying military actions and raising the stakes for regional stability. On Friday, Israel's cabinet authorized the mobilization of up to 75,000 reservists, signaling a potential ground invasion of Gaza following a rocket attack on Jerusalem, the first such attack in decades. The rocket, fired by Hamas, landed in the West Bank, and another targeted Tel Aviv, though it did not hit the city. The attack on Jerusalem stunned many Israelis, as the city has not been targeted by Palestinian rockets since 1970.

In response, Israel launched a major military campaign, including airstrikes and artillery attacks on Gaza, aiming to deter Hamas from launching cross-border attacks. The Israeli military reported that 97 rockets had been fired from Gaza into Israel on Friday, with 99 intercepted by the Iron Dome system. Dozens of Israeli bombing raids hit Gaza, including the destruction of the Gaza Interior Ministry building. The military also announced that two roads leading to Gaza would be off-limits to civilian traffic, indicating preparations for a possible ground operation.

Hamas claimed responsibility for the rocket attacks and warned that Israel should be aware of the "grave results" of a potential invasion. Meanwhile, Egypt's Prime Minister Hisham Kandil visited Gaza, expressing support for a truce and offering to mediate between Israel and Hamas. However, the three-hour truce declared during his visit did not hold, and tensions continued to rise.

The conflict has resulted in significant casualties, with at least 30 Palestinians killed in Gaza since Wednesday, including 13 militants and 16 civilians, among them eight children and a pregnant woman. On the Israeli side, three civilians were killed in Kiryat Malachi when a rocket struck an apartment building. The Israeli military also reported the killing of Hamas commander Ahmed Jabari in an airstrike, marking a major blow to the group.

The conflict has drawn international attention, with the United Nations and the Nonaligned Movement condemning Israel's actions as disproportionate and aggressive. The U.S. has called on Arab countries with ties to Hamas to urge the group to stop its rocket attacks, while reaffirming its support for Israel's right to defend itself. Egypt, under President Mohamed Morsi, has taken a more active role in the crisis, sending its prime minister to Gaza to mediate and offering humanitarian support.

The situation remains volatile, with fears that the conflict could escalate further
